summary: Describes the EPP mapping for provisioning and managing Internet domain names in a shared registry. It defines how EPP commands apply to domain names, written in XML. It was replaced by RFC 4931.

eli5.summary: This part of the registry language says how to ask for a new web address, change who runs it, or drop it.

subtitle: How to provision and manage domain names using EPP.

tldr.problem: Domain registries need a standard way to apply EPP operations specifically to domain names, including managing nameservers, renewal periods, contacts, and transfer policies.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines how to use EPP commands (create, delete, check, info, transfer, update, renew) and responses specifically for domain objects, with XML elements for domain attributes like nameservers, registration periods, and authorization information.
tldr.outcome: Registrars and registries can provision domain names interoperably using a common protocol. RFC 4931 supersedes this specification.

sections.title: EPP for Domain Names
sections.content:
This document defines how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (RFC 3730) applies to domain name objects. It specifies the XML structure and semantics for domain-specific EPP commands and responses. Understanding RFC 3730 (the base EPP specification) is essential for reading this document.

A domain object in EPP has attributes such as its fully qualified name, the contacts associated with it (registrant, administrative, technical, billing), the nameservers that provide DNS delegation, status values, and authorization information (typically a password for transfer). These attributes can be viewed and modified through EPP commands.
sections.eli5: This document is like an instruction manual for the domain name part of EPP. It says what information you can ask about or change for a domain name, and in what format you ask and answer.

sections.title: Domain Object Attributes
sections.content:
An EPP domain object is defined by several attributes. The domain name is a fully qualified name conforming to DNS naming rules (RFC 952 as updated by RFC 1123). The registrant is a contact object identifier for the person or organization that owns the domain. Administrative, technical, and billing contacts are additional contact object identifiers for people managing different aspects of the domain.

Nameservers can be specified in two ways: as references to existing host objects (preferred when host objects are supported), or as inline host attributes containing a hostname and optional IP addresses. Validity periods specify how long the domain registration lasts, measured in years or months, from 1 to 99 units. The authorization information (typically a password) protects the domain from unauthorized transfer requests. Status values describe the domain's current state: normal (ok), pending an action (pendingCreate, pendingDelete, etc.), or subject to restrictions (clientDeleteProhibited, clientTransferProhibited, etc.).
sections.eli5: A domain has several pieces of information: its name, who owns it and who manages it, which computers route its traffic, how long the registration lasts, a password to move it, and a status saying what you're allowed to do with it.

sections.title: Query Commands for Domains
sections.content:
The check command determines whether one or more domain names can be registered. The client sends a list of domain names; the server responds with the availability of each name and an optional reason if the name cannot be registered (e.g., "In use").

The info command retrieves detailed information about a domain, including its nameservers, contacts, creation and expiration dates, current status, and modification history. Authorization information (the transfer password) is only returned if the querying client is the sponsoring client or provides valid authorization credentials. An optional hosts attribute controls whether delegated hosts or subordinate hosts are returned.

The transfer query command retrieves the status of a pending domain transfer, including which client requested the transfer, when it was requested, which client must approve it, and the deadline for action.
sections.eli5: The read-only commands ask the registry three things: is this domain name available, what do you know about this domain, and what is the status of a domain transfer I started.

sections.title: Transform Commands for Domains
sections.content:
The create command creates a new domain object. The client specifies the domain name, an optional registration period (defaulting to the server's default if not specified), optional nameservers, a registrant contact, optional administrative/technical/billing contacts, and authorization information.

The delete command removes a domain from the registry. Servers typically require that subordinate host objects (e.g., ns1.example.com under example.com) be deleted or moved to another domain first.

The renew command extends the domain's registration period. The client must provide the current expiration date to prevent accidental double-renewal. The update command modifies domain attributes: it can add nameservers or contacts, remove them, or change the registrant or authorization information.

The transfer command manages changes in domain sponsorship. A client can request a transfer (with an optional period extension), cancel a pending transfer, or approve/reject a transfer request from another client. Transfers are protected by requiring authorization information. The sponsoring client is notified via a service message of pending transfers.
sections.eli5: The write commands ask the registry to create a new domain with nameservers and contacts, delete it, make it last longer, change its nameservers or contacts, or move it to a different registrar.

sections.title: Domain Status and Pending Operations
sections.content:
Domain objects carry status values that describe their condition. Status values prefixed with client can be set or removed by the sponsoring client. Status values prefixed with server are set or removed by the server. Other status values are server-managed only.

The ok status indicates a domain with no pending operations or prohibitions; it cannot be combined with any other status. clientDeleteProhibited and serverDeleteProhibited prohibit deletion requests. clientTransferProhibited and serverTransferProhibited prohibit transfer requests. clientUpdateProhibited and serverUpdateProhibited prohibit update requests. clientRenewProhibited and serverRenewProhibited prohibit renewal requests. clientHold and serverHold prevent the domain from being delegated in DNS.

Pending status values indicate an offline transform operation in progress. pendingCreate, pendingDelete, pendingRenew, pendingTransfer, and pendingUpdate all indicate that a server is processing the operation offline (for example, awaiting human review or third-party confirmation). When the operation completes, all affected clients are notified via service messages.
sections.eli5: Each domain has a status tag that says what you're allowed to do with it. Some tags are set by the owner, some by the registry. Other tags show that the registry is still processing a change request.

sections.title: Transfers and Authorization
sections.content:
Domain transfers are a core feature of EPP domain name management. A client can initiate a transfer request for any domain by providing the domain name and valid authorization information (transfer password). The current sponsoring client is notified and can approve or reject the request. If no action is taken within a server-defined grace period, the server may automatically approve or reject the request.

Transfer requests are coordinated through service messages in the EPP polling queue. The requesting client can cancel a request before the sponsoring client acts. The sponsoring client can also query the status of a pending transfer at any time.

Transfers of a domain implicitly transfer all subordinate host objects (e.g., ns1.example.com under example.com) to the new sponsoring client, preserving the integrity of domain object relationships. The transfer process may also extend the domain's registration period.
sections.eli5: Transferring a domain works like asking to borrow something from a friend: you give them the password to prove you have permission, the current owner gets a message asking whether to allow it, they can say yes or no, and if they don't answer in time, the system may decide automatically.
